authors: Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Søren Leth-Petersen, Torben Heien Nielsen and Tore Olsen
title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark
summary: Uses the universe of Danish savings records to show that tax subsidies for retirement accounts mostly shift saving between accounts: each krone of subsidy raises total saving by about one øre. Automatic employer contributions, by contrast, raise total saving almost one for one, because roughly 85 percent of individuals are passive savers who do not re-optimise.
data: Income tax register with third-party reported earnings and pension contributions (IND)
Third-party reported wealth: end-of-year assets and liabilities in taxable accounts
Population register (BEF)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
variables: Outcome: contributions to employer and individual retirement accounts
Outcome: taxable saving (change in taxable assets), gross and net
Treatment: employer pension contribution changes at job switches (automatic contributions)
Treatment: 1999 reduction in tax subsidy for capital pensions for top-bracket taxpayers (price subsidy)
Treatment: government mandatory savings plan (SP) contributions
sample_size: approximately 41 million observations for 4 million individuals
sample: Danish population aged 18–60, excluding observations with self-employment income (unbalanced panel).

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Camille Landais, Emmanuel Saez and Esben Schultz
title: Migration and Wage Effects of Taxing Top Earners: Evidence from the Foreigners' Tax Scheme in Denmark
summary: The 1991 preferential tax scheme for high-earning foreigners roughly doubled the number of highly paid foreigners in Denmark. The implied elasticity of migration with respect to the net-of-tax rate is above one, far larger than domestic labour supply elasticities, and the scheme generated modest wage spillovers.

Civil registration (CPR) citizenship and migration records with dates of entry and exit
Foreigners' tax scheme beneficiary records (contract start and end dates)
Employer links at firm and establishment level with industry

Outcome: number of foreigners above vs below the earnings threshold (migration response)
Outcome: earnings of scheme beneficiaries (wage effects / bunching at the threshold)
Outcome: spillovers on native top earners' employment and earnings
Key variable: citizenship and years of presence in Denmark
sample: All foreigners and natives resident in Denmark, focusing on foreigners with earnings around the scheme eligibility threshold (researchers excluded).

authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Kristian Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven and Gabriel Zucman
title: Wealth Taxation and Wealth Accumulation: Theory and Evidence from Denmark
summary: Exploits the 1989 Danish wealth tax reform, which cut rates sharply for the wealthy, to estimate long-run effects of wealth taxes on wealth accumulation. Responses are sizable for the very wealthy (top one percent) and small for the moderately wealthy, with effects that keep growing over a decade.
data: Administrative wealth registry (third-party reported assets and debts, since 1980)
Income registers and socio-economic registers (occupation, family composition)
variables: Outcome: log taxable wealth and third-party reported wealth
Treatment: 1989 wealth tax cut (unbound vs bound by tax ceiling: ceiling DD)
Treatment: doubling of couples' exemption threshold (couples DD)

Controls: pre-reform portfolio shares and income deciles
sample_size: 138,384 observations (ceiling DD) and 520,452 observations (couples DD, couples vs couples)
sample: Balanced panels of Danish households in the top 1% (ceiling DD) or married couples in the top 5% (couples DD) of the wealth distribution before the 1989 reform.

authors: Morten Bennedsen, Kasper Meisner Nielsen, Francisco Pérez-González and Daniel Wolfenzon
title: Inside the Family Firm: The Role of Families in Succession Decisions and Performance
summary: Uses the gender of a departing CEO's first-born child as an instrument for family succession in Danish firms. Family CEOs hurt performance: operating profitability falls by at least four percentage points relative to firms that hire outside CEOs, with the largest costs in fast-growing industries and large firms.

Danish Civil Registration System (CPR) with family links
Danish Commerce and Companies Agency (Erhvervs- og Selskabsstyrelsen) management/board records with CPR numbers
Industry-level data from Statistics Denmark and OECD STAN
variables: Outcome: operating return on assets (OROA) around CEO transitions
Treatment: family CEO succession (incoming CEO related by blood or marriage)
Instrument: gender of the departing CEO's firstborn child
Heterogeneity: industry growth, skill intensity and firm size
sample_size: 5,334 successions
sample: CEO successions in Danish limited liability (public and private) firms between 1994 and 2002, first transition per firm.

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Martin B. Knudsen, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Pedersen and Emmanuel Saez
title: Unwilling or Unable to Cheat? Evidence from a Tax Audit Experiment in Denmark
summary: A randomised field experiment with the Danish tax authority on about 40,000 taxpayers. Evasion is close to zero for third-party reported income but substantial for self-reported income, and audit threat letters raise reported self-reported income. Information, not morality, is what makes modern tax systems work.

SKAT Business Object Database: third-party information reports, pre-populated returns, filed returns and after-audit returns, item by item
SKAT computer-generated audit flags
Basic socio-economic variables and employer industry/size from SKAT records

Treatment: random threat-of-audit letters (100%, 50%, none) before the 2008 filing deadline
Outcome: detected tax evasion (audit adjustments to net income and tax)
Outcome: change in reported income in the following year
Heterogeneity: self-reported vs third-party reported income

sample: Stratified random sample of Danish taxpayers (employees, including transfer recipients, and self-employed) selected by SKAT for the audit experiment.

authors: Rasmus Lentz and Dale T. Mortensen
title: An Empirical Model of Growth Through Product Innovation
summary: Estimates a Schumpeterian model of firm growth through product innovation on a Danish firm panel. Reallocation of labour from less to more innovative firms accounts for roughly half of aggregate productivity growth, with the remainder coming from innovation within firms.
data: Danish Business Statistics Register: annual panel of privately owned firms (value added, total wage bill, full-time equivalent employment)
variables: Firm value added (Y)
Total wage bill (W) used to build quality-adjusted employment
Full-time equivalent employment (N)
Labor productivity: value added per worker and per quality-adjusted worker
Moments: firm growth rates including exit, and productivity growth decomposition (within, between, cross, exit)
sample_size: unbalanced panel of 4,872 firms
sample: All privately owned Danish firms existing in 1992 with more than 20 workers, followed through 1997, excluding later entrants.

authors: Rasmus Lentz, Suphanit Piyapromdee and Jean-Marc Robin
title: The Anatomy of Sorting: Evidence from Danish Data
summary: Estimates a flexible model of worker and firm heterogeneity in wages and job mobility on Danish matched employer-employee data. Workers and firms sort positively, with sorting operating through both wages and non-wage amenities, and worker heterogeneity accounts for the bulk of wage dispersion.
data: Matched employer-employee register data (IDA) with annual wages
Weekly labour market spell/mobility data built from Statistics Denmark registers
variables: Outcome: log wage rate
Job-to-job mobility and transitions to and from non-employment (weekly)
Latent worker and firm types (finite mixture, classification EM)
Controls: gender, education, potential experience, tenure, calendar time
Sorting channels: job preferences, segmentation, layoffs, job finding
sample: Danish workers after completing education, employment spells starting before age 50, followed weekly across employers from 1987 to 2013 (read from the 2018 predecessor working paper).

authors: Jesper Bagger, François Fontaine, Fabien Postel-Vinay and Jean-Marc Robin
title: Tenure, Experience, Human Capital, and Wages: A Tractable Equilibrium Search Model of Wage Dynamics
summary: Builds and estimates an equilibrium search model with on-the-job search and human capital accumulation using Danish career histories. Human capital accumulation drives most early-career wage growth, while job-to-job mobility and employer competition explain the later part of wage profiles.

Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA): hourly wages, education, experience, ownership
ATP pension contributions used to measure actual experience since 1964

Key variable: job tenure and actual labour market experience
Key variable: firm productivity measured by value added (accounting data)
Key variable: job-to-job, employment-to-unemployment transitions (spell data)
Stratification: three schooling levels (7–11, 12–14, 15–20 years)

sample: Danish private-sector male workers born in 1948 or later, at least two years past graduation, with histories truncated at entry into retirement, self-employment, the public sector or industries lacking value-added data.

authors: Jesper Bagger and Rasmus Lentz
title: An Empirical Model of Wage Dispersion with Sorting
summary: Estimates an equilibrium search model with endogenous search intensity and two-sided heterogeneity on Danish matched data. Finds positive assortative matching between worker and firm productivity, and quantifies how much of wage dispersion is due to sorting versus search frictions.
data: Weekly labour market spell data from administrative registers (jobs reported to tax authorities, public transfers, mandatory pension contributions)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA): education, hourly wages and firm sector
variables: Outcome: hourly wage (last week of November)
Key variable: job-to-job transitions and unemployment spells
Estimated: worker skill and firm productivity types (sorting)
Decomposition: log-wage variance into worker heterogeneity, firm heterogeneity, frictions and sorting
sample_size: 6,815,884 observations; 782,951 individuals; 1,698,990 job spells; 117,847 firms (NBER 2014 version)
sample: Danish workers up to age 55, after labour market entry, never observed in public-sector employment, self-employment, retirement or agriculture.

authors: David Hummels, Rasmus Jørgensen, Jakob Munch and Chong Xiang
title: The Wage Effects of Offshoring: Evidence from Danish Matched Worker-Firm Data
summary: Links product-level firm imports and exports to worker wages. Offshoring raises wages of high-skilled workers and lowers wages of low-skilled workers within job spells, while exporting raises wages for all. Tasks that are routine or easily offshored lose the most.
data: Firm Statistics Register (FirmStat/FIRM)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Firm-worker link (FIDA)
Foreign Trade Statistics Register, Extrastat and Intrastat (UHDI)
UN COMTRADE world trade data for instruments
Firm accounts and other firm registers (Data Appendix)

Treatment: firm offshoring (imports of inputs)
Treatment: firm exports
Instruments: world export supply and world import demand shocks by product and country (COMTRADE) and transport costs
Heterogeneity: worker skill type (high vs low skilled)
Outcome: earnings losses of displaced workers
sample_size: about 1.95 million worker-firm-year and 9,800 firm-year observations
sample: Manufacturing workers in Danish firms that both import and export, excluding single-year job spells, workers changing skill level, and firms with fewer than 50 employees and less than 0.6 million DKK in imports.

authors: Søren Leth-Petersen
title: Intertemporal Consumption and Credit Constraints: Does Total Expenditure Respond to an Exogenous Shock to Credit?
summary: The 1992 reform that let Danish homeowners borrow against housing equity provides an exogenous credit shock. Total expenditure responded only modestly on average, with the response concentrated among young households with little liquid wealth, which indicates that credit constraints bind for a minority.
data: Income tax register: taxable income, transfers, final taxes
Wealth tax register: third-party reported assets and liabilities (housing, shares, mortgage deeds, cash, bonds, debt)
Administrative registers on family composition and dwelling characteristics
Danish Family Expenditure Survey (DES) 1994–1996, used to validate the expenditure imputation

Treatment: 1992 credit market reform allowing home equity to be used as collateral for consumption loans
Treatment group: homeowners (renters as comparison/consistency check)
Credit-constraint proxy: low liquid (non-housing) assets in 1991 relative to monthly disposable income

sample: Households from a 10% random sample of the Danish population, aged 18–75, not self-employed, non-movers observed in all years 1987–1996.

authors: Thais Lærkholm Jensen and Niels Johannesen
title: The Consumption Effects of the 2007–2008 Financial Crisis: Evidence from Households in Denmark
summary: Customers of banks that were hit hard by the crisis cut consumption more than customers of healthier banks. The channel is reduced credit availability: exposed households borrowed less and spent less, which shows how bank distress transmits to the real economy through households.
data: Tax authority third-party reports of all individuals' loan and deposit account balances, linked to bank identity via branch numbers (Nets lists)
Bank balance sheet data from the Danish Central Bank (MFI statistics)
Administrative registers on demographics, education, labour market and income
Income and wealth registers (capital income, social transfers, stock portfolios, pension accounts)
Motor vehicle register and real estate register

Outcome: individual borrowing (loan balances by account)
Outcome: imputed spending = disposable income minus change in net wealth
Outcome: car ownership (motor vehicle register)
Separate analysis: customers of banks that failed 2008–2011
sample_size: around 440,000 individuals, almost 3.5 million individual-years and more than 5.7 million individual-account-years
sample: 25% random sample of non-self-employed Danish residents aged 20–50 in 2007 whose primary bank did not fail during 2008–2011.

authors: Steffen Andersen, John Y. Campbell, Kasper Meisner Nielsen and Tarun Ramadorai
title: Sources of Inaction in Household Finance: Evidence from the Danish Mortgage Market
summary: Many Danish households fail to refinance fixed-rate mortgages when it is clearly profitable. A model with inattention and psychological refinancing costs fits the data, and both frictions are stronger for households with less education, income and financial wealth.
data: Loan-level mortgage data for all Danish mortgages from Danmarks Nationalbank (via mortgage bank associations)
Civil Registration System / population register (CPR/BEF) for demographics and household links
Income and wealth data from the Danish Tax Authority (SKAT) (IND/formue)
Education register (UDDA)

Incentive: financial gain from refinancing given coupon and market rates
Structural parameters: probability of inattention and psychological refinancing cost
Household characteristics: age, education, income, housing and financial wealth
sample_size: 2,376,815 household observations (9,351,183 household-quarters); 378,421 refinancings

authors: Annette Alstadsæter, Niels Johannesen and Gabriel Zucman
title: Tax Evasion and Inequality
summary: Matches leaked offshore account data (HSBC Switzerland, Panama Papers) and tax amnesty records to Scandinavian wealth registers. Tax evasion rises steeply with wealth: the top 0.01 percent evade about a quarter of their taxes, which materially raises measured top wealth shares.

Panama Papers / Mossack Fonseca leak matched to Norwegian and Swedish wealth data (not Denmark)
Tax amnesty voluntary disclosures in Norway and Sweden

National accounts household wealth totals

Ranking variable: household net wealth including imputed pension wealth

sample: Scandinavian households appearing in offshore leaks or tax amnesties, ranked in the full population wealth distribution, combined with Danish random audits.

authors: Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Family Health Behaviors
summary: A severe health shock to one family member, such as a heart attack or stroke, makes spouses and adult children raise their own preventive behaviour: more check-ups, more preventive medication and lifestyle changes. Responses are sharp, immediate and persistent, and they reflect updating about one's own risk.
data: Prescription Drug Database (LMDB), 1995–2011
Health Insurance Registry (SSR, primary-care and specialist contacts), 1985–2011
National Patient Registry (LPR), inpatient 1980–2011 and outpatient 1994–2011
Cause of Death Registry (DAR)

authors: Anna Piil Damm and Christian Dustmann
title: Does Growing Up in a High Crime Neighborhood Affect Youth Criminal Behavior?
summary: Refugees arriving between 1986 and 1998 were allocated to municipalities quasi-randomly. Boys placed in neighbourhoods with a higher share of youth criminals were later more likely to be convicted, especially for violent crime, which identifies a causal neighbourhood effect on criminal behaviour.

Administrative registers: age, residence, parents' IDs, country of origin, immigrant status and date of immigration
Educational Institution Register and surveys
Municipality-level crime and socio-economic measures built from the registers

Identification: quasi-random assignment of refugee families under the 1986–1998 spatial dispersal policy
Outcome: criminal conviction and charge between ages 15 and 21 (by crime type)
Longer-term outcomes: education and employment
Controls: family background, country of origin, municipality characteristics at assignment
sample_size: 4,425 children
sample: Refugee children from eight source countries who arrived in Denmark before age 15 with at least one refugee parent between 1986 and 1998 and are observed to age 21.

authors: Christian Dustmann, Kristine Vasiljeva and Anna Piil Damm
title: Refugee Migration and Electoral Outcomes
summary: Using the quasi-random refugee dispersal policy, refugee allocation raised vote shares for anti-immigration parties in rural municipalities and lowered them in the largest urban municipalities. Effects are strongest where refugees are few relative to natives and where crime rises after allocation.
data: Population register (BEF) to identify refugees and municipality of initial placement
Income, education, labour force and socio-economic registers for 1985 municipality characteristics

authors: Kristoffer B. Hvidberg, Claus T. Kreiner and Stefanie Stantcheva
title: Social Positions and Fairness Views on Inequality
summary: Links a large survey to income registers to compare perceived and actual positions in the income distribution and within reference groups (co-workers, neighbours, schoolmates). People misperceive their rank, fairness views depend on the perceived gap to others, and showing people their true position changes their views.

authors: Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Children and Gender Inequality: Evidence from Denmark
summary: Event studies around the birth of the first child show mothers' earnings fall about 20 percent relative to fathers' in the long run, through hours, participation and wage rates. These child penalties now account for most of the remaining gender earnings gap and are transmitted across generations through mothers' own upbringing.

Family and generational links (population register)

Matched employer-employee data (firm family-friendliness)

authors: Mette Foged and Giovanni Peri
title: Immigrants' Effect on Native Workers: New Analysis on Longitudinal Data
summary: Refugee-country immigration into Danish municipalities from 1991 to 2008 pushed less-educated native workers toward more complex, less manual occupations. Native wages and employment rose rather than fell, and effects were positive even for low-skilled natives who moved across firms.

Occupation codes linked to O*NET task intensities (manual, communication, cognitive)

authors: Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Family Labor Supply Responses to Severe Health Shocks: Evidence from Danish Administrative Records
summary: Compares households hit by a fatal versus a non-fatal health shock at the same time. After a spouse's death the surviving spouse raises labour supply to self-insure, while after a non-fatal shock spouses reduce labour supply to care for the patient. Children of the household adjust less.

National Patient Registry (LPR) hospitalisation records with ICD diagnoses

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven and Esben Anton Schultz
title: Estimating Taxable Income Responses Using Danish Tax Reforms
summary: Uses a series of Danish tax reforms between 1984 and 2005 and full-population tax records to estimate the elasticity of taxable income. Elasticities are small for labour income (around 0.05) and larger for capital income and for top earners, and they are larger for big reforms than small ones.

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Peer Ebbesen Skov
title: Tax Reforms and Intertemporal Shifting of Wage Income: Evidence from Danish Monthly Payroll Records
summary: The 2010 cut in the top marginal tax rate was announced in advance, and monthly payroll data show top earners shifting wage income from December 2009 into January 2010. Shifting is concentrated among managers and employees of small firms, and it inflates short-run elasticity estimates.

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, David Dreyer Lassen and Søren Leth-Petersen
title: Liquidity Constraint Tightness and Consumer Responses to Fiscal Stimulus Policy
summary: The 2009 payout of Special Pension savings worked as a fiscal stimulus. Measuring constraint tightness by the marginal interest rate households pay, the spending response is highest for households facing high marginal rates and otherwise small, which supports targeting stimulus at the credit constrained.

authors: Helena Skyt Nielsen, Torben Sørensen and Christopher Taber
title: Estimating the Effect of Student Aid on College Enrollment: Evidence from a Government Grant Policy Reform
summary: A 1988 reform raised Danish student grants for students from higher-income families. Roughly 1,000 dollars of extra aid raised enrolment by about 1.35 percentage points, a response that is consistent with modest credit constraints rather than binding ones.

authors: Christian Dustmann, Rasmus Landersø and Lars Højsgaard Andersen
title: Refugee Benefit Cuts
summary: A 2002 reform cut welfare benefits for newly arrived refugees by roughly half. Employment rose modestly in the short run and then faded, while disposable income fell sharply. The cut raised crime among adults and harmed children's school enrolment and outcomes.

Income register from tax authority records (earnings, transfers, taxes)
Hourly wage and occupation data
Labour market register (employment status)
Population register (BEF)

authors: Mette Ejrnæs and Stefan Hochguertel
title: Is Business Failure Due to Lack of Effort? Empirical Evidence from a Large Administrative Sample

Using a large administrative panel, insured entrepreneurs are more likely to close their businesses and enter unemployment, with effects that strengthen as the eligibility date approaches, consistent with reduced effort rather than selection alone.

title: Unemployment Insurance, Wage Dynamics and Inequality Over the Life Cycle
summary: Models permanent and transitory wage dynamics over the life cycle for Danish men, allowing dynamics to differ by unemployment insurance membership. title: Mathematics and Gender: Heterogeneity in Causes and Consequences

summary: Decomposes sibling correlations in permanent earnings, education and unemployment for the Danish population into family and community components, allowing for life-cycle dynamics. title: Gender Differences in Negotiation: Evidence from Real Estate Transactions
summary: Men appear to secure better prices than women in Danish real estate transactions, but the gap shrinks with better controls for property value and disappears in repeat-sales and inherited-property samples. title: Neighbourhood Gangs, Crime Spillovers and Teenage Motherhood
summary: Uses the random assignment of refugees to municipalities between 1986 and 1998. summary: Shows that the achievement gap by polygenic score for educational attainment is as large as the gap by socioeconomic status and widens during elementary school, but only among low-SES children. Spousal education is complementary in generating marital surplus, education stabilises marriages, education raises men's share of the surplus, and divorce costs are high both early and late in a marriage.

title: Measurement Error in Income and Schooling and the Bias of Linear Estimators
summary: Links survey reports of income and schooling for Danish respondents to the same variables in the registers. authors: Pieter Gautier, Paul Muller, Bas van der Klaauw, Michael Rosholm and Michael Svarer
title: Estimating Equilibrium Effects of Job Search Assistance

title: Birth Order and Delinquency: Evidence from Denmark and Florida
summary: In both Denmark and Florida, second-born boys are substantially more likely than their first-born brothers to be disciplined in school and to enter the criminal justice system. The evidence points to reduced parental time investment for later-born children, rather than differences in health at birth or neighbourhood, as the mechanism.

summary: Shows that the assumptions needed to identify returns to unordered treatments, such as fields of study, have testable implications, and characterises the bias when they fail. Using admission cut-offs and applicants' ranked choices in Denmark and Norway, payoffs to fields are strongly correlated across the two countries once fields violating the assumptions are dropped.
data: Danish administrative data on all applications to post-secondary education 1994–2002 (coordinated admission system)
Population register and other registers (background, completed field of study, annual earnings)
Norwegian post-secondary application data 1998–2004 linked to registers (comparison country)
variables: Outcome: annual earnings eight years after application (wages, self-employment and income-replacing transfers)
Treatment: completed field of study (nine broad fields)
Instrument: application score just above vs below the admission cutoff of the preferred field
Preferred and next-best field from applicants' rankings
period: Applications 1994–2002 (Denmark), outcomes eight years after application
sample: First-time applicants to Danish post-secondary education without a prior post-secondary degree who applied to at least two broad fields, with the preferred field having an admission cutoff, and who completed a field within eight years (paralleled with Norwegian applicants).

authors: Anders Frederiksen, Takao Kato and Nina Smith
title: Working Hours, Top Management Appointments, and Gender: Evidence from Linked Employer-Employee Data
summary: Links the Danish Labour Force Survey's detailed hours to register career histories. Long hours, hours relative to peers and nonstandard hours raise the odds of a top management appointment within the firm, and the gender gap in hours, driven mainly by supply-side factors, is a major contributor to the gender gap in reaching top management.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Danish Labour Force Survey (DLFS/AKU) linked on person identifier
Organizational hierarchy codes (occupation-based) from registers
variables: Outcome: appointment to a top management position between year t and t+1
Explanatory: weekly working hours from the Labour Force Survey in year t
Heterogeneity: gender (gender gap in hours and promotions)
Hierarchy level: top manager, manager, white-collar, blue/grey-collar
Controls: experience, tenure, education, children, marital status
sample_size: 168,499 employees
sample: Danish employees randomly sampled in the Labour Force Survey 1994–2010, merged with IDA register data (IZA DP 11675 working-paper version).

authors: Frederik Almar, Benjamin Friedrich, Ana Reynoso, Bastian Schulz and Rune Vejlin
title: Educational Ambition, Marital Sorting, and Inequality
summary: Classifies detailed Danish education programmes into ambition types by their graduates' starting wages and wage growth. Assortative matching by educational ambition has risen sharply even though sorting by conventional education levels looks flat, and the marriage market accounts for more than 40 percent of the rise in household income inequality since 1980.
data: Population register with partner links (BEF)
Education register with four-digit ISCED programme codes (UDDA)
Employment register with hourly wages (IDAN)
Income register (IND)
Danish Labour Force Survey (LFS/AKU), 2000–2018
Employment register for hours, part-time/full-time (RAS)
variables: Classification: educational 'ambition types' from programme-level starting wages and wage growth (about 1,800 programmes)
Outcome: marital sorting by ambition type (assortative matching)
Outcome: household labour income inequality
Wage measure: residualised log hourly wages by programme
LFS job attributes: hours, evening/weekend/home work
sample_size: on average 3,031,511 individuals per year aged 19–60; 1,800,866 individuals in couples per year
sample: All individuals living in Denmark aged 19–60 in 1980–2018, with couples defined as married or cohabiting opposite-sex partners.

authors: Michael Svarer, Michael Rosholm and Jakob Roland Munch
title: Rent Control and Unemployment Duration
summary: Uses Danish register data on unemployment spells and housing to study whether living in rent-controlled housing affects job finding. Unemployed workers in rent-controlled dwellings have lower exit rates from unemployment, consistent with rent control reducing geographic mobility.
data: 10% random sample of the Danish adult population from administrative registers (Statistics Denmark)
Housing unit characteristics for dwellings occupied by the sample
Weekly labour market event histories
Danish Tax Authorities 1999 hedonic model for owner-occupied housing (to predict uncontrolled rent)
variables: Outcome: unemployment duration in weeks (exit to job in local vs national labour market)
Explanatory: rent control benefit decile (predicted uncontrolled rent minus actual rent), time-varying
Mobility: job finding with move to another of 51 commuting areas
Tenure type: private rental housing vs other
sample_size: 14,645 persons contributing 31,966 unemployment spells
sample: Inflow sample of unemployment spells 1997–2000 from a 10% random sample of the Danish adult population (IZA DP 842 working-paper version).

authors: Paul Bingley and Gauthier Lanot
title: Public Pension Programmes and the Retirement of Married Couples in Denmark
summary: Estimates a dynamic discrete choice model of couples' joint retirement and saving on a 1 percent register sample of Danish couples, using the introduction and reforms of the early retirement programme (efterløn) for identification. Retirement responds asymmetrically for men and women to their own and their spouse's income flows.
data: 1% sample of Danish couples of potential retirement age from an administrative register
variables: Outcome: retirement decisions of husband and wife (joint retirement)
Identifying variation: introduction and subsequent reforms of the publicly financed early retirement programme (efterløn)
Explanatory: own and spouse's income flows
Model: dynamic discrete choice model with saving
sample: A 1% register sample of Danish married couples of potential retirement age.

authors: Brian Krogh Graversen and Jan C. van Ours
title: How to Help Unemployed Find Jobs Quickly: Experimental Evidence from a Mandatory Activation Program
summary: A randomised experiment in two Danish counties assigned newly unemployed workers to an intensive activation programme with early job search courses, frequent meetings and mandatory activation. Treated workers found jobs substantially faster, with the threat of mandatory activation an important part of the effect.
data: Public Employment Service (PES) administrative registers (treatment status, demographics, meetings with caseworkers)
DREAM weekly register of public income transfers (Danish National Labour Market Authority)
variables: Outcome: unemployment duration in weeks / job finding rate
Treatment: random assignment to mandatory activation programme by birth date (born 1st–15th of month)
Mechanism: meetings with caseworkers, job search programmes, training programmes
Exit states: employment, other benefits, right-censoring
sample_size: 4,520 unemployment spells (2,229 treatment, 2,291 control)
sample: Newly unemployed UI benefit recipients registering at the PES in Storstrøm and South Jutland counties between November 2005 and February 2006, first spell only.

authors: Nabanita Datta Gupta and Marianne Simonsen
title: Non-cognitive Child Outcomes and Universal High Quality Child Care
summary: Links the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children to the registers to compare non-cognitive outcomes at age seven for children in universal preschool, family day care and home care at age three. Attending high-quality preschool does not harm non-cognitive outcomes relative to home care, while long hours in family day care are associated with worse outcomes for some groups.
data: Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC), waves 1996, 1999, 2003
Administrative registers on parents' education, labour market status, hours, wages and income (1994–2003)
Day Care Register (Statistics Denmark), used descriptively
variables: Outcome: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) index at age 7½
Treatment: mode of care at age 3½ (preschool, family day care, home care)
Instrument/pseudo-experiment: municipality differences in childcare take-up and provision
Heterogeneity: child gender and mother's education
Hours in non-parental care
sample_size: 4,343 observations (children) in the main OLS estimates
sample: About 6,000 Danish children born between 15 September and 31 October 1995 surveyed in DALSC, linked to parental register data.

authors: Daniel le Maire and Bertel Schjerning
title: Tax Bunching, Income Shifting and Self-Employment
summary: Self-employed Danes bunch sharply at the top tax kink, but much of the bunching reflects intertemporal shifting of income through retained earnings in the business rather than real changes in effort. Accounting for shifting implies a much smaller elasticity of real income.
data: Tax records of Danish self-employed individuals (taxable income, retained earnings)
variables: Outcome: bunching of taxable income at kinks of the tax schedule
Mechanism: intertemporal income shifting via retained earnings in the business tax schemes
Estimate: taxable income elasticity (0.43–0.53 ignoring shifting; structural 0.14–0.20)
sample: Danish self-employed taxpayers.

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Jakob Roland Munch and Hans Jørgen Whitta-Jacobsen
title: Taxation and the Long Run Allocation of Labor: Theory and Danish Evidence
summary: Estimates a search model with non-linear taxation, in which workers keep looking for better-paid jobs, on employer-employee register data for all Danish workers and workplaces in 2004 to 2006. Danish taxes reduce total income by about 12 percent through the allocation of labour across jobs, and moving to low-tax OECD levels would recover four fifths of the loss.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken) for hours-adjusted wages (robustness)
Empirical effective marginal tax rate schedule for 2006 from Kleven and Kreiner (2006)
variables: Workplace average hourly wage rate (annual labour income / annual hours)
Workplace size, number of stayers and new hires (job-to-job flows)
New hires from non-employment
Effective marginal tax rates by income level (used to estimate structural search model and efficiency loss)
sample_size: 126,400 workplaces employing 1.4 million workers
sample: Full population of private-sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005 and their workers aged 18–65, with wages between DKK 90 and DKK 714 per hour.

authors: Juanna Schrøter Joensen and Helena Skyt Nielsen
title: Spillovers in Education Choice
summary: Exploits the Danish high school pilot that made advanced mathematics cheaper to take for some cohorts. An older sibling's advanced maths choice raises the probability that the younger sibling also chooses advanced maths, with spillovers that depend on the siblings' gender composition.
data: Danish administrative registers on high school enrolment, course packages and completion (Statistics Denmark education registers)
Parent and sibling links from population registers
Parental education and income registers
Earnings registers (younger siblings' earnings at ages 30–35)
variables: Outcome: younger sibling chooses advanced math-science course package in high school
Endogenous regressor: older sibling's advanced math-science choice
Instrument: older sibling enrolled in a high school that unexpectedly introduced the pilot scheme (PilotIntro)
Outcomes: younger sibling's college/STEM education at age 30 and log earnings at ages 30–35
Controls: parental education and income, county and entry-cohort fixed effects
period: High school entry cohorts 1984–1987 (older siblings) and 1988–1991 (younger siblings, main sample); register data from 1980 onwards
sample_size: 7,786 sibling pairs (main closely spaced sample); 17,691 sibling pairs in the wider sample with age gap < 10 years
sample: Older siblings entering academic high school 1984–1987 who graduated in three years, paired with younger siblings entering high school 1988–1991 with an age gap of at most 4 years.

authors: Maya Rossin-Slater and Miriam Wüst
title: Parental Responses to Child Support Obligations: Evidence from Administrative Data
summary: Uses discontinuities in the Danish child support schedule by fathers' income to estimate how higher obligations affect separated parents. The paper documents responses in fathers' income, subsequent family formation and the parents' living arrangements.
data: Danish administrative registers on children born 1985–2008 linked to parents and siblings (population/family registers)
Income and tax records including tax-deductible child support payments
Labour market registers (employment, earnings, disability insurance, early retirement)
Birth records (fertility through 2010)
Education registers
Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC) and Children and Youth in Denmark (CYD) survey (descriptive, supplementary)
variables: Treatment: father's average child support obligation (from Danish child support guideline schedule)
Identifying variation: income thresholds in the child support guidelines (simulated instrument)
Outcome: father's annual child support payment
Outcome: father–child co-residence (physical custody)
Outcomes: post-separation fertility and labour supply of both parents
sample_size: 73,303 fathers (71,575 unique mothers)
sample: Fathers observed every year 1998–2010 who separated from their oldest child's mother (or had a first child while not cohabiting) in 1999–2008, with one or two children under 18 and separation-year income near the first three guideline thresholds.

authors: Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Labor Supply and Optimization Frictions: Evidence from the Danish Student Labor Market
summary: Danish students lose part of their study grant when annual earnings exceed a threshold. Register data show bunching below the threshold that grows as students gain experience with the rule, so optimisation frictions hide a structural elasticity well above the observed response.
data: Danish administrative registers for the full population (education, earnings, benefits, demographics)
Annual income tax returns
Monthly student benefit (SU) take-up records from the Student Benefit Administration
Monthly payroll records of earnings and hours (BFL/eIndkomst), from 2008
variables: Outcome: annual labour earnings relative to the student benefit income limit (bunching)
Incentive: kink/notch from phase-out (payback) of student grants above the individual income limit
Simulated individual marginal tax and phase-out rates
Monthly earnings and benefit take-up (timing of adjustment)
sample_size: around 75,000 observations per year (core sample 75,500 individuals per year on average)
sample: Individuals aged 18–35 enrolled in tertiary education, fully eligible for student benefits and with positive labour earnings (above DKK 8,000 per year).

authors: N. Meltem Daysal, Michael Lovenheim, Nikolaj Siersbæk and David N. Wasser
title: Home Prices, Fertility, and Early-Life Health Outcomes
summary: For Danish homeowners aged 20 to 44, a 100,000 kroner rise in home prices raises the probability of giving birth by about 2.35 percent. Birth outcomes improve too, but mostly because of who gives birth, and there is no effect on children's health in the first five years.
data: Medical Birth Register (MFR)
National Patient Register (LPR)
State's Sales and Valuation Registry (public property valuations and sales prices)
Population register (BEF) and other registers for demographics, education, household income and partner status
variables: Treatment: once-lagged one-year change in estimated home value (public valuation adjusted by local sale-price ratio)
Outcome: indicator for giving birth
Outcomes: birth weight, low birth weight, very low birth weight, prematurity
Outcomes: hospital admissions, ER visits and days hospitalised in first year and ages 1–5
Comparison group: renters
sample_size: 1,105,559 observations on 198,435 women (125,903 births)
sample: Women aged 20–44 who became first-time homeowners between 1993 and 2004, purchasing between ages 18 and 42.

authors: Marianne Simonsen, Lars Skipper, Niels Skipper and Anne Illemann Christensen
title: Spot Price Biases in Non-Linear Health Insurance Contracts
summary: The Danish prescription drug reimbursement scheme has coverage that rises with annual spending and resets each year. Consumers look forward-looking around the reset but react too strongly to current prices within the year, and liquidity constraints rather than plan literacy or cognitive decline explain the spot-price bias.
data: Population-wide individual data on prescription drug purchases and reimbursement under the Danish non-linear drug insurance scheme (registers not named in the abstract)
variables: Incentive: spot price of drugs as a non-linear function of year-to-date spending
Incentive: end-of-year reset of the coverage (deductible) year
Outcome: timing and amount of prescription drug purchases
Heterogeneity: liquidity constraints, plan literacy, cognitive decline
sample: Population-wide data on Danish consumers of prescription drugs covered by the non-linear reimbursement scheme (details not available from the abstract).

authors: Katrine Jakobsen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Identifying Behavioral Responses to Tax Reforms: New Insights and a New Approach
summary: Shows that standard estimates of taxable income elasticities from tax reforms are biased by mean reversion and diverging income trends across the distribution, and proposes an approach that exploits reform timing to separate behavioural responses from these trends, applied to Danish tax reforms.
data: Danish administrative registers for the full population since 1980 (labour market history, education, earnings, demographics)
Third-party reported income tax records
Simulated marginal tax rates from an extended Danish tax simulator (Kleven and Schultz 2014 model)
variables: Outcome: changes in taxable income (broad, personal, labour income) over four-year periods
Treatment: predicted change in log net-of-tax rate from the 2004 and 2009–10 Danish tax reforms
Income-bin dummies capturing trend differentials across the income distribution
Validation: income trends in parts of the distribution unaffected by the reform
period: Data since 1980; main analyses 1999–2012 (2004 reform: 1999–2003 pre-period, 2003–2007 reform period; 2009–10 reform: 2004–2008 pre-period, 2008–2012 reform period); 1987 and 1994 reforms in appendix
sample_size: over 2,000,000 individuals per period (2,240,332 and 2,295,922 for the 2004 reform pre-reform and reform periods; 2,097,862 and 2,240,833 for the 2009–10 reform)
sample: Individuals present in the tax data with positive income over each four-year period and initial personal income above DKK 200,000 (2004 reform) or DKK 250,000 (2009–10 reform), about half the Danish adult population.

authors: Mette Foged, Linea Hasager, Giovanni Peri, Jacob Nielsen Arendt and Iben Bolvig
title: Intergenerational Spillover Effects of Language Training for Refugees
summary: Follows the children of refugees affected by the 1999 Danish reform that improved language training. Children of treated parents achieve better educational outcomes, showing that the integration gains from language training carry over to the next generation.
data: Danish administrative registers from Statistics Denmark on refugees' asylum/admission dates and parent–child links
Lower secondary school completion and final exam records
Criminal conviction records (property, violent, narcotics crime)
Earnings, occupation (ISCO), disposable income, marriage and fertility registers for parents
variables: Running variable: parent's admission (asylum grant) date relative to 1 January 1999 (Integration Act language training reform)
Outcome: completing lower secondary school and taking final exams by age 18
Outcome: criminal convictions between ages 15 and 18
Parental outcomes: annual earnings, complex job, disposable income, convictions
period: Children born 1990–2001, followed up to 2019; parental outcomes 1999–2016
sample_size: 6,467 children; 5,197 adult parents
sample: Children born 1990–2001 with at least one parent granted asylum in Denmark within a four-year window around 1 January 1999, who arrived before or during primary school age.

authors: Sofie Cairo and Robert Mahlstedt
title: The Disparate Effects of Information Provision: A Field Experiment on the Work Incentives of Social Welfare
summary: A field experiment in Denmark informed welfare recipients about a minimum work requirement, either with personalised running counts of their hours or with generic rules. Personalised information raised employment among those below the required hours, while generic notices reduced labour supply among those at low near-term risk of sanctions.
data: Field experiment assignment and messaging data (Danish public employment service, jobnet.dk online tool)
Population registers (socio-demographic background)
Benefit payment records (DREAM)
Monthly income and employment records (eIndkomst/BFL)
Public employment service data on sanctions, exemptions, collected working hours, click data and registered job applications
variables: Treatment: random assignment to personalised online information tool about benefit-reduction risk under the work requirement (three arms)
Outcome: employment and earnings
Outcome: welfare benefit receipt and exit to alternative income support
Outcome: working hours collected toward the requirement and job applications
Heterogeneity: job search activity and sanction risk
period: Intervention from 15 August 2018 with up to five monthly reminders
sample_size: 47,294 individuals
sample: All Danish welfare benefit recipients on 15 August 2018 subject to the 225-hour work requirement who had received the official notification letter.

authors: Hans Schytte Sigaard
title: Estimating Labor Supply Responses to Danish Tax Reforms
summary: Applies taxable income elasticity methods to register data on hours actually worked. The intensive-margin labour supply elasticity is about 0.08, close to the labour income and taxable income elasticities, and it comes from changes in contract hours, paid absence and switches between main and secondary jobs.
data: Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken, LON) for performed hours of work
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDAN) for workplace controls
Income registers (IND, INDK, INPI) for marginal tax rate simulation
Population register (BEF) and family income register (FAIN)
Family register (FAMILIE)
Education register (UDDA)
Danish tax simulation programs (Kleven and Schultz 2014, extended by the Ministry of Finance)
variables: Outcome: three-year log change in annual performed hours of work
Treatment: three-year log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate on labour income
Instrument: mechanical (simulated) change in marginal tax rate from tax reforms, using lagged income
Secondary outcomes: labour income and taxable income
Controls: income splines, socio-economic and municipality controls
sample_size: 10,755,733 observations
sample: Employed wage earners aged 25–65 covered by the Wage Statistics Register with positive hours in both years of each three-year difference and base-year labour income above DKK 250,000.

authors: Esteban García-Miralles and Jonathan M. Leganza
title: Joint Retirement of Couples: Evidence from Discontinuities in Denmark
summary: Uses age discontinuities in eligibility for Danish early retirement and public pensions to show that when one spouse becomes eligible and retires, the other spouse is substantially more likely to retire as well, quantifying spillovers that matter for evaluating retirement reforms.
data: Danish administrative registers for the full population 1986–2014 (labour market outcomes, pension benefits, socio-demographics, family/couple links)
Annual taxable earnings registers
Monthly earnings records for all employees (eIndkomst/BFL) and monthly pension benefit records, from 2008
Voluntary early retirement pension (VERP) contribution records
variables: Outcome: spouse's retirement (ceasing to earn labour income)
Outcome: pension claiming (VERP or OAP) and annual labour earnings
Running variable (age-based design): reference individual's age relative to early pension eligibility age 60
Running variable (reform-based design): birth date relative to 1 January 1954 cutoff of the 2011 reform raising VERP eligibility age by 6 months

sample: Dual-earner Danish couples (married, registered partners or cohabiting) up to 8 years apart in age, with the reference individual aged 57–60, excluding self-employed and disability recipients.

authors: Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Jack Blundell
title: Income Effects and Labour Supply: Evidence from a Child Benefits Reform
summary: A 2011 Danish cap on child benefits cut payments to families with several young children and left smaller families unaffected. Mothers' labour supply rises substantially after the cut, mainly on the extensive margin, and sterilisation records are used to control for differences in preferences for more children.
data: Population register (BEF) for family composition, marital status and cohabitation
Monthly payroll records with hours worked (BFL/eIndkomst)
Child benefit payment records (BOBO/BOTI)
Register OF (monthly demographics and parental leave status)
Sterilisation consultations from the National Patient Register (LPRADM) and health insurance service registers (SYSI, SSSY)
Annual income register (IND) for self-employment robustness
variables: Treatment: 2011 cap on child benefits (DKK 35,000) reducing unearned income for larger families with young children
Outcome: monthly hours worked (intensive and extensive margins)
Outcome: annual earnings (robustness incl. self-employed)
Control/restriction: family sterilisation consultation before the reform
Design: difference-in-differences, treated vs unaffected families
sample_size: 28,968 treated women and 22,477 treated men
sample: Native Danish married or cohabiting parents aged 25–59 over the window with 2–4 children (at least two under 18) in January 2011, not self-employed, observed in a balanced monthly panel.

authors: Linea Hasager
title: Does Granting Refugee Status to Family-Reunified Women Improve Their Integration?
summary: Women who enter Denmark through family reunification usually hold permits that depend on staying married. Granting them independent refugee status improves their economic integration, raises divorce rates and lowers the risk of violence against them, consistent with reduced residency uncertainty and greater bargaining power.
data: Admission register on immigrant status and residence permit application/approval dates (Danish Immigration Service data via Statistics Denmark)
Labour market data from the Danish tax authorities (employment; hours and earnings from 2008)
Police registers on victimisation and criminal convictions
Hospital admissions data (National Patient Register) for assault injuries
Central population register (BEF) for demographics, spouse links and divorce
variables: Treatment: family-reunified woman granted her own refugee status (asylum), staggered timing
Outcome: quarterly employment, hours of work and earnings
Outcome: victimisation of violence (police records or assault-related hospitalisation)
Outcome: divorce
Design: staggered difference-in-differences with not-yet-treated women as controls
sample_size: 1,349 adult women
sample: Women aged 18+ who were family-reunified to a refugee spouse in Denmark between 2001 and 2017 and later applied for and obtained their own refugee status.

authors: Thomas Høgholm Jørgensen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: The Division of Parental Leave: Empirical Evidence and Policy Design
summary: Uses sharp incentives in the Danish parental leave benefit system for about 190,000 births to estimate parents' willingness to pay for leave. Parents bunch at kinks and are willing to pay for a traditional split with little leave for fathers, and simulations show that earmarked leave works much better when combined with high replacement rates.
data: Parental leave benefit spell data (parents of children born 2008–2015), incl. benefits paid to parent or employer
Monthly earnings records for all employees (BFL/eIndkomst), from 2008
Danish administrative registers on demographics, family links and firm links (population and labour market registers)
variables: Outcome: weeks of parental leave taken by mother and father within three years of birth
Incentive: individual benefit replacement rates and benefit cap creating kinks in the household budget set
Incentive: employer-provided full wage compensation (from benefits paid to employer)
Policy: earmarked (father quota) leave and replacement rate counterfactuals in a structural model
sample_size: 189,974 births
sample: Births 2008–2015 to parents in stable employment and not on non-birth public benefits in the three months before birth, excluding births followed by another child within 15 months.

authors: Linea Hasager and Mia Jørgensen
title: Sick of Your Poor Neighborhood? Quasi-Experimental Evidence on Neighborhood Effects on Health
summary: Uses the quasi-random dispersal of refugees across Danish neighbourhoods from 1986 to 1998. Refugees placed in low-income neighbourhoods had a 12 percent higher risk of developing a lifestyle-related disease 8 to 15 years later, driven by neighbours and the local environment rather than health care access, ethnic networks or labour market outcomes.
data: National Patient Register (LPR)
Health Insurance Register (SYSI, SSSY)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Income register (IND)
Population register (BEF) and address/mobility registers (BEFBOP, BEFADR)
Migration register (VNDS)
Criminal convictions register (KRAF)
O*NET occupational data merged via occupation codes

Outcome: lifestyle-related disease diagnosis (circulatory, nutritional/metabolic, COPD, hip arthrosis, alcohol-related) 2–15 and 8–15 years after immigration

Mechanisms: health care access, employment and earnings, neighbour characteristics
